claim: Crystal structures of PPARγ have revealed overlapping binding modes for synthetic and natural/endogenous ligands, indicating competition for the orthosteric pocket.
source: Crystal structures of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) have revealed overlapping binding modes for synthetic and natural/endogenous ligands, indicating competition for the orthosteric pocket.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by references to prior structural studies throughout the manuscript.

claim: Cobinding of a synthetic ligand to the orthosteric pocket can push natural and endogenous PPARγ ligands (fatty acids) out of the orthosteric pocket towards an alternate ligand-binding site near the Ω-loop.
source: Here we show that cobinding of a synthetic ligand to the orthosteric pocket can push natural and endogenous PPARγ ligands (fatty acids) out of the orthosteric pocket towards an alternate ligand-binding site near the functionally important omega (Ω)-loop.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by X-ray crystallography, NMR, MD simulations, and functional assays described throughout the manuscript.

claim: Synthetic ligand and fatty acid cobinding can form a 'ligand link' to the Ω-loop and synergistically affect the structure and function of PPARγ.
source: X-ray crystallography, NMR spectroscopy, all-atom molecular dynamics simulations, and mutagenesis coupled to quantitative biochemical functional and cellular assays reveal that synthetic ligand and fatty acid cobinding can form a 'ligand link' to the Ω-loop and synergistically affect the structure and function of PPARγ.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental techniques described in the abstract and detailed in the results section.

claim: Ligand binding to nuclear receptors can be more complex than the classical one-for-one orthosteric exchange of a natural or endogenous ligand with a synthetic ligand.
source: These findings contribute to a growing body of evidence indicating ligand binding to nuclear receptors can be more complex than the classical one-for-one orthosteric exchange of a natural or endogenous ligand with a synthetic ligand.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study and is supported by the data presented.

claim: TZDs are synthetic agonists of PPARγ with potent anti-diabetic efficacy in patients with type 2 diabetes.
source: Thiazolidinediones (TZDs), also called glitazones, are synthetic agonists of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) nuclear receptor with potent anti-diabetic efficacy in patients with type 2 diabetes (Soccio et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: TZDs were initially discovered in phenotypic screens as compounds with anti-diabetic efficacy.
source: TZDs were initially discovered in phenotypic screens as compounds with anti-diabetic efficacy (Fujita et al., 1983), and later studies identified PPARγ as the molecular target (Lehmann et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citations.

claim: PPARγ was identified as the molecular target of TZDs in later studies.
source: TZDs were initially discovered in phenotypic screens as compounds with anti-diabetic efficacy (Fujita et al., 1983), and later studies identified PPARγ as the molecular target (Lehmann et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by a citation.

claim: The use of TZDs in diabetic patients has dropped significantly due to adverse side effects, including bone loss and water retention.
source: After an increase in clinical use of TZD drugs such as rosiglitazone (Avandia) in the early 2000s, the use of TZDs in diabetic patients has dropped significantly due to adverse side effects, including bone loss and water retention.
evidence: This is a known clinical observation.

claim: The PPARγ ligand-binding pocket is among the largest in the nuclear receptor superfamily, ranging from 1200 to 1400 Å3 in crystal structures.
source: The PPARγ ligand-binding pocket (Figure 1A) is among the largest in the nuclear receptor superfamily (Gallastegui et al., 2015), ranging from 1200 to 1400 Å3 in crystal structures with three branches described as 'T' or 'Y' shaped (Kroker and Bruning, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: The PPARγ ligand-binding pocket has three branches described as 'T' or 'Y' shaped.
source: The PPARγ ligand-binding pocket (Figure 1A) is among the largest in the nuclear receptor superfamily (Gallastegui et al., 2015), ranging from 1200 to 1400 Å3 in crystal structures with three branches described as 'T' or 'Y' shaped (Kroker and Bruning, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Branch I of the PPARγ ligand-binding pocket is located proximal to helix 12.
source: Branch I is located proximal to helix 12, which forms a critical part of the activation function-2 (AF-2) coregulator binding surface
evidence: This is a structural description based on crystal structures.

claim: Branch II of the PPARγ ligand-binding pocket is located near the β-sheet surface, close to the predicted ligand entry/exit site.
source: branch II is located near the β-sheet surface, close to the predicted ligand entry/exit site where helix 3 meets helix 6 and the helix 11/12 loop
evidence: This is a structural description based on crystal structures.

claim: Branch III of the PPARγ ligand-binding pocket is located near the β-sheet surface but deeper in the pocket near helix 5.
source: branch III is also located near the β-sheet surface but deeper in the pocket near helix 5 (Edman et al., 2015; Aci-Sèche et al., 2011; Genest et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a structural description supported by citations.

claim: One of the first crystal structures of PPARγ was solved bound to rosiglitazone.
source: One of the first crystal structures of PPARγ was solved bound to the synthetic TZD ligand rosiglitazone (Nolte et al., 1998), which revealed critical details on the molecular contacts formed between a ligand and the binding pocket of the receptor.
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by a citation.

claim: Crystal structures of PPARγ bound to dietary MCFAs and long-chain UFAs revealed overlapping binding modes with synthetic ligands that occupy all three branches of the orthosteric pocket.
source: Subsequent crystal structures of PPARγ bound to dietary medium-chain fatty acids (MCFAs) and long-chain unsaturated fatty acids (UFAs), the latter of which are endogenous PPARγ ligands (Kim et al., 2011), revealed overlapping binding modes with synthetic ligands that occupy all three branches of the orthosteric pocket (Kroker and Bruning, 2015; Itoh et al., 2008; Li et al., 2008a; Waku et al., 2009a; Waku et al., 2009b; Malapaka et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior structural studies.

claim: Synthetic and natural ligands compete for binding to the same orthosteric pocket of PPARγ.
source: These crystal structures and others, combined with biochemical ligand displacement assays (Kliewer et al., 1997; Ziouzenkova et al., 2003; Xu et al., 1999; Nagy et al., 1998), revealed that synthetic and natural ligands compete for binding to the same orthosteric pocket.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural and biochemical studies.

claim: Synthetic PPARγ ligands can also bind to an alternate site distinct from the orthosteric pocket.
source: However, recent studies have shown that synthetic PPARγ ligands that were originally designed to bind to the orthosteric pocket can also bind to an alternate site (Hughes et al., 2016; Li et al., 2008b; Hughes et al., 2014; Brust et al., 2017; Jang et al., 2017; Bae et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claim: The alternate site partially overlaps with branch II of the orthosteric pocket and uniquely occupies space in a solvent exposed pocket formed by the flexible Ω-loop.
source: The alternate site partially overlaps with one of the arms of the T/Y-shaped orthosteric pocket near the β-sheet surface (branch II), but it uniquely occupies space in a solvent exposed pocket formed by the flexible Ω-loop that precedes helix 3 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a structural description supported by Figure 1B.

claim: Ligand occupancy of branch I within the orthosteric pocket is linked to robust stabilization of the AF-2 surface and increased 'classical' transcriptional activation.
source: Structural studies have linked ligand occupancy of branch I (i.e., the helix 12 subpocket) within the orthosteric pocket to robust stabilization of the AF-2 surface, increased 'classical' transcriptional activation, and side effects associated with TZDs in part driven by hydrogen bonds formed between the TZD head group and residues within branch I (Choi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Ligands that bind to a combination of branch II and the alternate site can stabilize the Ω-loop region.
source: In contrast, ligands that either do not form hydrogen bonds in the helix 12/branch I subpocket, or bind to a combination of branch II and the alternate site, can stabilize the Ω-loop region and a nearby loop.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from structural studies.

claim: Stabilization of the Ω-loop region can inhibit phosphorylation of S273 by the Cdk5 kinase and is associated with anti-diabetic efficacy.
source: Stabilization of this region near the Ω-loop can inhibit phosphorylation of a serine residue (S273 in PPARγ isoform one or S245 in isoform 2) by the Cdk5 kinase and is associated with anti-diabetic efficacy (Jang et al., 2017; Bae et al., 2016; Choi et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Edaglitazone contains a bulky benzo[b]thiophene group adjacent to the TZD head group.
source: Edaglitazone contains a bulky benzo[b]thiophene group adjacent to the TZD head group, in contrast to other TZD-bound PPARγ crystal structures, which have smaller moieties (e.g., phenyl) adjacent to the TZD head group.
evidence: This is a description of the chemical structure of edaglitazone.

claim: The crystal structure of PPARγ LBD bound to edaglitazone revealed a bacterial MCFA cobound to the alternate site.
source: We solved the crystal structure of the PPARγ LBD bound to edaglitazone at the orthosteric pocket, which unexpectedly revealed a bacterial MCFA cobound to the alternate site.
evidence: This is a finding from the crystal structure determination.

claim: MCFAs are dietary mammalian natural PPARγ ligands obtained from foods such as oils and dairy products.
source: MCFAs are not only bacterial lipids; they are also dietary mammalian natural PPARγ ligands obtained from foods such as oils and dairy products (Rial et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: MCFAs display high serum concentrations (µM–mM) that activate PPARγ transcription.
source: MCFAs display high serum concentrations (µM–mM) that activate PPARγ transcription; regulate the expression of PPARγ target genes; and influence cellular differentiation, adipogenesis, and insulin sensitization in mice (Malapaka et al., 2012; Liberato et al., 2012; Nagao and Yanagita, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Crystal structures of PPARγ bound to covalent orthosteric antagonists revealed that synthetic ligand extensions within the orthosteric pocket can push fatty acid cobinding modes towards the Ω-loop.
source: The cobound MCFA provides a 'ligand link' to the flexible Ω-loop, and crystal structures of PPARγ bound to covalent orthosteric antagonists revealed that synthetic ligands extensions within the orthosteric pocket can push fatty acid cobinding modes towards the Ω-loop.
evidence: This is a finding from the crystal structure determination.

claim: Endogenous UFAs can be pushed from their orthosteric binding modes to an alternate site cobinding mode when a synthetic TZD ligand binds to the orthosteric pocket.
source: Inspired by these findings, we solved several crystal structures showing that endogenous UFAs can be pushed from their orthosteric binding modes to an alternate site cobinding mode when a synthetic TZD ligand binds to the orthosteric pocket.
evidence: This is a finding from the crystal structure determination.

claim: Cobinding of a synthetic ligand and fatty acid affects the conformation of the AF-2 surface and synergistically enhances coactivator interaction.
source: Using NMR spectroscopy, molecular dynamics simulations, isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC), and mutagenesis coupled to functional assays, we show that cobinding of a synthetic ligand and fatty acid affects the conformation of the AF-2 surface, synergistically enhances coactivator interaction, and may affect PPARγ transcription in cells.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental techniques described in the manuscript.

claim: Edaglitazone and rosiglitazone display similar affinities for PPARγ, 141 nM and 93 nM respectively, in a fluorescent tracer ligand displacement assay.
source: Edaglitazone and rosiglitazone display similar affinities for PPARγ, 141 nM and 93 nM respectively, in a fluorescent tracer ligand displacement assay (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is data from a TR-FRET ligand displacement assay shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Edaglitazone and rosiglitazone show similar potencies in a TR-FRET biochemical assay on increasing the interaction of a TRAP220 coactivator peptide (132 nM and 186 nM respectively).
source: The compounds also show similar potencies in a TR-FRET biochemical assay on increasing the interaction of a peptide derived from the TRAP220 coactivator (Figure 2C; 132 nM and 186 nM respectively)
evidence: This is data from a TR-FRET coregulator interaction assay shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Edaglitazone and rosiglitazone show similar potencies in decreasing the interaction with a NCoR corepressor peptide (171 nM and 432 nM respectively).
source: and decreasing the interaction with a peptide derived from the NCoR corepressor (Figure 2D; 171 nM and 432 nM respectively)
evidence: This is data from a TR-FRET coregulator interaction assay shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Edaglitazone and rosiglitazone show similar potencies in a cell-based transcriptional reporter assay (5.4 nM and 3.2 nM respectively).
source: as well as in a cell-based transcriptional reporter assay (Figure 2E; 5.4 nM and 3.2 nM respectively).
evidence: This is data from a cell-based luciferase reporter assay shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The crystal structure of edaglitazone-bound PPARγ LBD was solved at 2.1 Å resolution.
source: The structure was solved at 2.1 Å (Table 1) as a homodimer with two molecules in the asymmetric unit (chains A and B) with the expected alpha helical sandwich fold.
evidence: This is data from X-ray crystallography.

claim: In the edaglitazone-bound structure, both chains adopt an active helix 12 conformation.
source: However, in our edaglitazone-bound structure, both chains adopt an active helix 12 conformation (Figure 3A) with nearly identical backbone conformations (Cα r.m.s.d. 0.186 Å).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Strong electron density was observed for three ligands in both chain A and B molecules of the edaglitazone-bound structure: one edaglitazone bound to the canonical orthosteric pocket, a second edaglitazone to a surface pocket, and a MCFA consistent with C9 bound to a solvent accessible region near helix 3, the β-sheet surface, and the Ω-loop region.
source: Strong electron density was observed for three ligands in both chain A and B molecules (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1): one edaglitazone bound to the canonical or orthosteric pocket; a second edaglitazone to a surface pocket created through an interaction between two symmetry-related protein molecules (Figure 3—figure supplement 2); and a MCFA consistent with the size of a nonanoic acid (C9) molecule bound to a solvent accessible region near helix 3, the β-sheet surface of the orthosteric pocket, and the flexible Ω-loop region.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 3B and supplementary figures.

claim: PPARγ expressed in E. coli can retain MCFAs from the bacteria, predominately C9, which function as natural PPARγ agonists.
source: Notably, a previous study showed that PPARγ expressed in E. coli can retain MCFAs from the bacteria, predominately C9, which function as natural PPARγ agonists (Malapaka et al., 2012; Liberato et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: When bound to the orthosteric pocket, rosiglitazone and edaglitazone make conserved hydrogen bonds via the TZD head group to the side chains of S289, H323, H449, and Y473.
source: When bound to the orthosteric pocket, rosiglitazone (Figure 3C) and edaglitazone (Figure 3D) make conserved hydrogen bonds via the TZD head group to the side chains of S289 (helix 3), H323 (helix 5), H449 (helix 10/11), and Y473 (helix 12).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structures shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: The TZD head group of rosiglitazone makes a hydrogen bond to Q286, which is not present in the edaglitazone-bound structure.
source: The TZD head group of rosiglitazone also makes a hydrogen bond to Q286 (helix 3), which is not present in the edaglitazone-bound structure due to a 2.8 Å shift of the Q286 side chain from the rosiglitazone-bound position (5.7 Å away from the TZD 2-carbonyl position).
evidence: This is a structural observation from comparing the crystal structures.

claim: In the edaglitazone-bound structure, F363 and M364 undergo shifts of 6.0 Å and 2.6 Å respectively away from the ligand-binding pocket to accommodate the benzo[b]thiophene.
source: These residues undergo a shift of 6.0 Å (Phe363) and 2.6 Å (M364) away from the ligand-binding pocket to accommodate the benzo[b]thiophene in the edaglitazone-bound structure, along with several other subtler changes (<1 Å) that accommodate 5-methyl-2-phenyloxazole tail group near the β-sheet (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A previous study reported a crystal structure of PPARγ LBD with three molecules of C9 in the orthosteric pocket.
source: A previous study reported a crystal structure of PPARγ LBD that was obtained using protein purified from E. coli, which revealed the presence of bound endogenous bacterial MCFAs (Liberato et al., 2012). Specifically, three molecules of C9 were observed in the orthosteric pocket (Figure 4A) overlapping in space where edaglitazone is bound in our structure (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and comparison to the current structure shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Analysis of electron density maps for previously published crystal structures of PPARγ bound to rosiglitazone (PDB: 1FM6) and MCC-555 (PDB: 3B0Q) revealed extra unidentified densities suggesting a MCFA could be bound.
source: Analysis of the electron density maps deposited to the PDB for two relatively high resolution (~2 Å) crystal structures bound to rosiglitazone (PDB: 1FM6) and MCC-555 (PDB: 3B0Q) revealed extra unidentified densities suggesting there could be a MCFA bound in a similar manner to what we observed in the edaglitazone structure.
evidence: This is based on re-analysis of previously deposited crystallographic data.

claim: In a crystal structure of RXRα-PPARγ LBD heterodimer bound to rosiglitazone (PDB: 1FM6), replacement of two water molecules with C9 better describes the density.
source: In a crystal structure of RXRα-PPARγ LBD heterodimer where PPARγ was bound to rosiglitazone (PDB: 1FM6) solved to 2.1 Å (Gampe et al., 2000), two water molecules were modeled next to rosiglitazone where the C9 is bound in our edaglitazone structure (Figure 4C). We found that replacement of the water molecules with a C9 better describes the density in this region (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on re-modeling of a previously published crystal structure, shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: Density consistent with a MCFA was found in crystal structures of PPARγ bound to GQ-16 and SR145.
source: Additionally, we found density consistent with a MCFA in crystal structures of PPARγ bound to GQ-16 (Figure 4G) and SR145 (Figure 4H), which had been solved to 2.1 Å and 2.2 Å, respectively (Bruning et al., 2007; Amato et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on re-analysis of previously published crystal structures, shown in Figures 4G and 4H.

claim: Differential 2D [1H,15N]-TROSY HSQC NMR analysis of native and delipidated PPARγ LBD revealed subtle chemical shift and peak intensity/line broadening changes.
source: To determine the degree to which bacterial MCFAs are bound to PPARγ, we performed differential 2D [1H,15N]-TROSY HSQC NMR analysis of 15N-labeled PPARγ LBD subjected to a delipidation protocol and 'native' protein that was not subjected to delipidation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), which revealed subtle chemical shift and peak intensity/line broadening changes.
evidence: This is data from NMR spectroscopy shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Titration of C9 into native PPARγ caused additional selective NMR chemical shift changes, indicating that native protein is likely only partially bound to bacterial MCFAs.
source: Notably, titration of C9 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) into native PPARγ caused additional selective NMR chemical shift changes, indicating that native protein is likely only partially bound to (i.e., is not saturated with) bacterial MCFAs.
evidence: This is data from NMR spectroscopy shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Differential NMR analysis of rosiglitazone-bound forms of native and delipidated PPARγ revealed subtle NMR chemical shift perturbations for residues near the C9 bound to the alternate site.
source: We also performed differential NMR analysis of rosiglitazone-bound forms of native and delipidated PPARγ to determine if there could be cobinding of a synthetic TZD to native protein bound to a substoichiometric amount of a bacterial MCFA. Although the NMR spectra overlay very closely (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), subtle NMR chemical shift perturbations were observed for a select number of peaks (Figure 5A), including residues in our crystal structure near the C9 bound to the alternate site on helix 3 (V277, Q283, and G284), as well as residues within the AF-2 surface on helix 5 (L317 and K319) and helix 12 (L465, I472, and K474).
evidence: This is data from NMR spectroscopy shown in Figures 5A and 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Titration of C9 into rosiglitazone-bound native or delipidated PPARγ revealed NMR chemical shift perturbations for residues affected in the differential analysis of rosiglitazone bound to native or delipidated forms without added C9.
source: We next performed differential NMR analysis to determine if exogenously added MCFAs, which are dietary components of the mammalian diet, can cobind with synthetic ligands to PPARγ. We titrated C9 into rosiglitazone-bound native PPARγ (Figure 5B) and delipidated PPARγ (Figure 5C) and again performed differential NMR analysis. The binding affinity of C9 (Figure 5—figure supplement 4) is ~50,000 fold weaker than rosiglitazone; thus, to eliminate competition for the orthosteric pocket, we titrated one and three molar equivalents of C9 into PPARγ pretreated with two molar equivalents of rosiglitazone. This analysis again revealed subtle NMR chemical shift perturbations for essentially the same residues that were affected in the differential analysis of rosiglitazone bound to native or delipidated forms without added C9 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is data from NMR spectroscopy shown in Figures 5A, 5B, 5C, and 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The direction of the chemical shift change that occurs upon titration of C9 to rosiglitazone-bound native or delipidated PPARγ is the same direction of the shift that occurs when comparing rosiglitazone-bound native and delipidated PPARγ without added C9.
source: Notably, the direction of the chemical shift change that occurs upon titration of C9 to rosiglitazone-bound native (Figure 5B) or delipidated (Figure 5C) PPARγ is the same direction of the shift that occurs when comparing rosiglitazone-bound native and delipidated PPARγ without added C9 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an observation from NMR data shown in Figures 5A, 5B, and 5C.

claim: The peak position of rosiglitazone-bound native PPARγ shows a 'head start' in shifting compared to delipidated PPARγ, which supports that native rosiglitazone-bound PPARγ is bound to a substoichiometric amount of MCFA.
source: In fact, the peak position of rosiglitazone-bound native PPARγ shows a 'head start' in shifting compared to delipidated PPARγ, which further supports that native rosiglitazone-bound PPARγ is bound to a substoichiometric amount of MCFA.
evidence: This is an interpretation of NMR data.

claim: Similar shifting of NMR peaks was observed for edaglitazone-bound PPARγ upon C9 titration.
source: We observed a similar shifting of peaks for edaglitazone-bound PPARγ (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is data from NMR spectroscopy shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Only very minor shifting is observed for the H323 NMR peak when C9 is titrated into rosiglitazone-bound PPARγ, supporting cobinding rather than orthosteric competition.
source: If C9 was competing with rosiglitazone bound to the orthosteric pocket, residues near the TZD head group such as H323, which forms a side chain-mediated hydrogen bond with the aromatic TZD head group, would likely shift significantly. Aromatic ring current effects, which have a significant influence on NMR peak positions, would change in this portion of the orthosteric pocket if C9 displaced rosiglitazone. However, only very minor shifting is observed for the H323 NMR peak as compared to the larger shifting that occurs for residues near the bound C9 in our crystal structure.
evidence: This is an observation from NMR data that supports the cobinding model.

claim: NMR peaks affected by C9 binding to PPARγ in the absence of rosiglitazone are not affected in the cobinding experiments with rosiglitazone, supporting cobinding rather than orthosteric competition.
source: Furthermore, other NMR peaks affected by C9 binding to PPARγ in the absence of rosiglitazone are not affected in the cobinding experiments with rosiglitazone, nor do they move from the rosiglitazone-bound peak position to the C9-bound peak position (Figure 5—figure supplement 5). These observations support the cobinding of C9, not orthosteric competition of C9, under our experimental conditions.
evidence: This is an observation from NMR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5 that supports the cobinding model.

claim: Two microsecond molecular dynamics simulations were conducted with edaglitazone bound to the orthosteric pocket in the absence or presence of C9 at the alternate site.
source: Two microsecond simulations were conducted with edaglitazone bound to the orthosteric pocket in the absence or presence of C9 at the alternate site. For each ligand-bound state, two replicate simulations on the chain A and B crystallized conformations were performed resulting in a total of eight stable simulations (Figure 6A) allowing averaging of up to four simulations for each state.
evidence: This describes the molecular dynamics simulation setup, with results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In all eight molecular dynamics simulations, edaglitazone remained stably bound to the orthosteric pocket.
source: In all eight simulations, edaglitazone remained stably bound to the orthosteric pocket (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a result from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 6B.

claim: C9 remained stably bound to the alternate site in three out of four simulations with edaglitazone cobound to the orthosteric pocket.
source: C9 remained stably bound to the alternate site in three out of four simulations with edaglitazone cobound to the orthosteric pocket (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a result from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 6C.

claim: When cobound to C9, Ω-loop conformational fluctuations show a broader range of smaller R.M.S.D. values (2–5 Å) with a notable increase in the 2–4 Å range relative to edaglitazone bound alone.
source: Conformational fluctuations in the Ω-loop when bound to edaglitazone alone, calculated as the coordinate R.M.S.D. relative to the crystallized conformation after minimization and equilibration, range between 4–6 Å (Figure 6D). However, when cobound to C9, Ω-loop conformational fluctuations show a broader range of smaller R.M.S.D. values (2–5 Å) with a notable increase in the 2–4 Å range relative to edaglitazone bound alone.
evidence: This is a result from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 6D.

claim: A conformational stabilizing effect is observed for Ω-loop residues that contact the cobound C9.
source: Thus, a conformational stabilizing effect is observed for Ω-loop residues that contact the cobound C9.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the molecular dynamics simulation results.

claim: The loop connecting helix 1 and helix 2a, which contains S245, shows reduced conformational fluctuation when cobound to C9 relative to edaglitazone bound alone.
source: The loop connecting helix 1 and helix 2a, which is proximal to the Ω-loop and contains a residue (S245 in PPARγ1; S273 in PPARγ2) that is phosphorylated by the kinase Cdk5 (Choi et al., 2010), also shows reduced conformational fluctuation when cobound to C9 relative to edaglitazone bound alone (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a result from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 6E.

claim: C9 cobinding to the alternate site stabilizes the conformation of helix 12, which shows decreased R.M.S.D. values relative to edaglitazone bound alone.
source: Finally, C9 cobinding to the alternate site stabilizes the conformation of helix 12, which shows decreased R.M.S.D. values relative to edaglitazone bound alone (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a result from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Several hydrogen bonds between the carboxylate head group of C9 and various backbone and side chain groups of PPARγ were observed in molecular dynamics simulations.
source: Several hydrogen bonds between the carboxylate head group of C9 and various backbone and side chain groups of PPARγ were observed in all three simulations (Figure 7A), and among these the hydrogen bonds to the K265 backbone and S342 side chain were also observed in the crystal structure.
evidence: This is a result from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A complex network of water-bridged hydrogen bonds was observed in molecular dynamics simulations, including water-mediated hydrogen bonds linking the oxazole nitrogen atom in edaglitazone to the carboxylate head group of C9.
source: Notably, a complex network of water-bridged hydrogen bonds was observed (Figure 7B), including several different types of water-mediated hydrogen bonds linking the oxazole nitrogen atom in edaglitazone to the carboxylate head group of C9 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a result from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figures 7B and 7C.

claim: A network of hydrophobic interactions was observed in molecular dynamics simulations, including interactions between the terminal phenyl group of edaglitazone and the saturated carbon side chain of C9.
source: In addition to these hydrogen bonds, a network of hydrophobic interactions was observed in all three simulations (Figure 7D), including the side chains of L255, F264, V277, R280, I281, F287, and the terminal phenyl group of edaglitazone interacts with the saturated carbon side chain of C9 (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a result from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figures 7D and 7E.

claim: GW9662 is an antagonist that covalently binds to C285 and blocks ligand binding to the orthosteric pocket.
source: GW9662 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) is an antagonist that covalently binds to C285 located in, and blocks ligand binding to, the orthosteric pocket (Leesnitzer et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Structural superposition of GW9662-bound PPARγ (PDB: 3B0R) with C9-bound PPARγ (PDB: 4EMA) revealed that GW9662 overlaps with two out of the three crystallized C9 binding modes in branches I and III.
source: Structural superposition of an available crystal structure of GW9662-bound PPARγ (PDB: 3B0R) with a crystal structure of PPARγ bound to C9 (32) (PDB: 4EMA) revealed that GW9662 overlaps with two out of the three crystallized C9 binding modes in branches I and III (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a structural comparison shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Crystal structures of PPARγ bound to GW9662 and SR16832 were solved at 2.29 Å and 2.73 Å, respectively.
source: We solved two new crystal structures of PPARγ bound to GW9662 and SR16832 (Brust et al., 2017), an analog of GW9662 that we developed with a ligand extension that weakens synthetic ligand binding to the alternate site (Brust et al., 2017), at 2.29 Å and 2.73 Å, respectively (Table 2).
evidence: This is data from X-ray crystallography.

claim: Electron density consistent with a bound bacterial MCFA was observed in crystal structures of PPARγ bound to GW9662 and SR16832.
source: Similar to our edaglitazone crystal structure, we observed electron density consistent with a bound bacterial MCFA in both structures, which we modeled as C9.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structures.

claim: In chain A of the GW9662-bound structure, one C9 is present within the branch II region of the orthosteric pocket; in chain B, there are two C9 molecules present, one in branch II and another closer to the cobound position in the edaglitazone structure.
source: In chain A of our GW9662-bound structure, one C9 is present within the branch II region of the orthosteric pocket; in chain B, there are two C9 molecules present, one in branch II and another closer to the cobound position in our edaglitazone structure (Figure 8B; Figure 8—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In the SR16832 structure, C9 is present only in chain A; and the 6-methoxyquinoline group extension in SR16832 appears to have blocked the branch II C9 binding mode, pushing the C9 closer to the cobound position in the edaglitazone structure.
source: In the SR16832 structure, C9 is present only in chain A; and the 6-methoxyquinoline group extension in SR16832, relative to GW9662, appears to have blocked the branch II C9 binding mode, pushing the C9 closer to the cobound position in our edaglitazone structure (Figure 8C; Figure 8—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Differential NMR analysis confirmed the C9 binding regions in the crystal structures of PPARγ bound to GW9662 and SR16832.
source: We performed differential NMR analysis to confirm the C9 binding regions in the crystal structures of PPARγ bound to GW9662 and SR16832. This analysis was limited relative to the analysis we performed above for rosiglitazone and edaglitazone because about half of the expected NMR peaks are missing due to intermediate exchange on the NMR time scale from significant µs–ms time scale dynamics present when bound to covalent antagonists relative to agonists that robustly stabilize the dynamics of PPARγ (Hughes et al., 2016; Hughes et al., 2014; Brust et al., 2017; Hughes et al., 2012; Marciano et al., 2015). Despite this limitation, chemical shift perturbations were observed for residues near the crystallized C9 binding modes observed in the GW9662 (Figure 8D) and SR16832 (Figure 8E) crystal structures, including residues on helix 2b/β-sheet surface such as I249, L255, G258, L340, G344, G346, and M348, confirming the crystallized C9 binding modes.
evidence: This is data from NMR spectroscopy shown in Figures 8D and 8E.

claim: Crystal structures of PPARγ LBD bound to AA or OA were solved to 2.1 and 1.95 Å, respectively.
source: To explore this hypothesis, we cocrystallized PPARγ LBD with AA or OA and solved two structures to 2.1 and 1.95 Å, respectively (Table 3).
evidence: This is data from X-ray crystallography.

claim: The crystal structures of PPARγ bound to AA or OA show two different UFA binding modes in the two chains present in the crystal structure.
source: The structures show two different UFA binding modes in the two chains present in the crystal structure: one where the acid group associates near helix 12 with the hydrophobic fatty acid tail projecting to the back portion of the pocket near the β-sheet surface (Figure 9A,B; Figure 9—figure supplement 1A,B); and a second where the acid head group adopts a different conformation flipped away from helix 12 with a similar hydrophobic tail conformation near the β-sheet (Figure 9—figure supplements 1A,B and and 2A,B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structures shown in Figures 9A, 9B, and supplementary figures.

claim: Crystal structures were solved of AA-bound PPARγ with GW9662, OA-bound PPARγ with GW9662, and OA-bound PPARγ with rosiglitazone to ~2.2 Å.
source: To determine if a synthetic ligand can cobind with the bound UFA, we soaked GW9662 or rosiglitazone into preformed UFA-bound crystals and were able to solve three crystal structures to ~2.2 Å (Table 3), including AA-bound PPARγ with GW9662 (Figure 9C; Figure 9—figure supplement 1C), OA-bound PPARγ with GW9662 (Figure 9D; Figure 9—figure supplement 1D), and OA-bound PPARγ with rosiglitazone (Figure 9E; Figure 9—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is data from X-ray crystallography shown in Figures 9C, 9D, 9E, and supplementary figures.

claim: The binding of GW9662 or rosiglitazone did not completely displace the bound endogenous UFA (AA or OA) but pushed the UFA towards the back of the pocket towards the Ω-loop to an alternate site.
source: The structures revealed that the binding of GW9662 or rosiglitazone did not completely displace the bound endogenous UFA (AA or OA). Instead, the binding of the synthetic ligands to UFA-bound PPARγ within the crystals pushed the bound UFA towards the back of the pocket towards the Ω-loop to an alternate site within the crystals (i.e., not the orthosteric binding mode obtained when the UFA was co-crystallized alone), which is apparent in structural overlays of the crystal structures of PPARγ bound to individual UFAs and cobound with GW9662 (Figure 9—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structures shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Differential NMR analysis confirmed cobinding of AA with GW9662-bound PPARγ.
source: We performed differential NMR analysis to confirm the ligand cobinding observed in the crystal structures. When PPARγ is bound to GW9662, addition of AA (Figure 9F) or OA (Figure 9G) caused selective NMR chemical shift perturbations for a similar set of residues affected in the C9 cobinding NMR experiments.
evidence: This is data from NMR spectroscopy shown in Figure 9F.

claim: Differential NMR analysis confirmed cobinding of OA with GW9662-bound PPARγ.
source: When PPARγ is bound to GW9662, addition of AA (Figure 9F) or OA (Figure 9G) caused selective NMR chemical shift perturbations for a similar set of residues affected in the C9 cobinding NMR experiments.
evidence: This is data from NMR spectroscopy shown in Figure 9G.

claim: NMR analysis showed that addition of OA to rosiglitazone-bound PPARγ caused selective chemical shift perturbations for residues in close proximity to the cobound OA molecule and within the AF-2 surface.
source: Furthermore, NMR analysis showed that addition of OA to rosiglitazone-bound PPARγ (Figure 9H) also caused selective chemical shift perturbations for residues in close proximity to the cobound OA molecule, including F226, G284, and S342; as well as residues within the AF-2 surface on helix 5 (L317 and K319) and helix 12 (K474).
evidence: This is data from NMR spectroscopy shown in Figure 9H.

claim: For wild-type PPARγ, three MCFAs (C9, C10, and C12) and two UFAs (AA and OA) caused a concentration dependent increase in the TRAP220 peptide interaction in a TR-FRET assay.
source: For wild-type PPARγ, three MCFAs including C9 (Figure 10A), decanoic acid (C10; Figure 10—figure supplement 1A), and dodecanoic acid (C12; Figure 10—figure supplement 1B) and two UFAs AA (Figure 10B) and OA (Figure 10C) caused a concentration dependent increase in the TRAP220 peptide interaction.
evidence: This is data from a TR-FRET biochemical assay shown in Figure 10A, 10B, 10C, and supplementary figures.

claim: When PPARγ was preincubated with GW9662, the fatty acids similarly caused a concentration-dependent increase in TRAP220 peptide interaction.
source: When PPARγ was preincubated with GW9662, the fatty acids similarly caused a concentration-dependent increase.
evidence: This is data from a TR-FRET biochemical assay.

claim: SR16832 preincubation lowered the assay window of activity; smaller MCFAs (C9 and C10) only showed a small increase in TRAP220 peptide interaction, whereas C12 and the endogenous UFAs, AA and OA, did not.
source: However, SR16832 preincubation lowered the assay window of activity to a large degree; smaller MCFAs (C9 and C10) only showed a small increase in TRAP220 peptide interaction, whereas C12 and the endogenous UFAs, AA and OA, did not.
evidence: This is data from a TR-FRET biochemical assay.

claim: MCFAs and UFAs binding to PPARγ when the orthosteric pocket is blocked by a covalent ligand can influence PPARγ function.
source: Taken together, these data show that MCFAs and UFAs binding to PPARγ when orthosteric pocket is blocked by a covalent ligand can influence PPARγ function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TR-FRET and FP assay data.

claim: C9 binding was more potent for SR16832-bound PPARγ compared to wild-type PPARγ or GW9662-bound PPARγ.
source: Compared to wild-type PPARγ or GW9662-bound PPARγ, we found that C9 binding was more potent for SR16832-bound PPARγ (Figure 10—figure supplement 3) despite the bulkier addition in SR16832, relative to GW9662, that points towards and blocks the branch II C9 binding mode (Brust et al., 2017).
evidence: This is data from a TR-FRET biochemical assay shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 3.

claim: The increased potency of C9 for SR16832-bound PPARγ is likely due to hydrogen bonds between the aryl ether/methoxy group of SR16832 with the carboxylate head group and other aliphatic protons in C9.
source: Inspection of the SR16832 crystal structure cobound to C9 indicated the increased potency is likely due to hydrogen bonds between the aryl ether/methoxy group of SR16832 with the carboxylate head group and other aliphatic protons in C9 (Figure 10—figure supplement 4), the latter of which can form weak hydrogen bonds with methoxy groups (Palusiak and Grabowski, 2002).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 4, supported by a citation.

claim: DFT calculations revealed a net attractive interaction between C9 and the SR16832 methoxy group (10.3 kcal/mol) and a repulsive interaction with the phenyl moiety of GW9662 (8.56 kcal/mol).
source: In support of this hydrogen bond network, we performed density functional theory (DFT) calculations, which revealed a net attractive interaction between C9 and the SR16832 methoxy group (10.3 kcal/mol) and a repulsive interaction with the phenyl moiety of GW9662 (8.56 kcal/mol).
evidence: This is data from DFT calculations.

claim: For C9, the R288A mutant decreased the efficacy more than the other single mutants without affecting potency to a large degree relative to wild-type PPARγ in a TR-FRET assay.
source: For C9, the R288A mutant (Figure 10A) decreased the efficacy (i.e., TR-FRET window) more than the other single mutants without affecting potency to a large degree relative to wild-type PPARγ.
evidence: This is data from a TR-FRET biochemical assay shown in Figure 10A.

claim: The R288A/S342A double mutant and the R288A/S342A/K265A triple mutant decreased both the potency and efficacy of C9 in a TR-FRET assay.
source: However, the R288A/S342A double mutant and the R288A/S342A/K265A triple mutant decreased both the potency and efficacy.
evidence: This is data from a TR-FRET biochemical assay.

claim: For AA and OA, the potency and efficacy was largely affected in the presence of the covalent ligands with the single mutants, and overall most affected for the double and triple mutants in a TR-FRET assay.
source: For AA (Figure 10B) and OA (Figure 10C), the potency and efficacy was largely affected in the presence of the covalent ligands with the single mutants, and overall most affected for the double and triple mutants.
evidence: This is data from a TR-FRET biochemical assay shown in Figures 10B and 10C.

claim: Residues R288, S342, and K265 are important for driving alternate site affinity and/or functional efficacy of cobound UFAs.
source: This indicates these residues are important for driving alternate site affinity and/or functional efficacy of cobound UFAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis and TR-FRET assay data.

claim: The affinity of the TRAP220 peptide was strengthened in the presence of C9 alone, and more so for OA alone, as measured by ITC.
source: The affinity of the TRAP220 peptide was strengthened in the presence of C9 alone, and more so for OA alone. Inspection of the fitted thermodynamic parameters shows this is driven by a favorable change in entropy (ΔS) in the fatty acid-bound state.
evidence: This is data from ITC experiments shown in Table 4.

claim: In the presence of edaglitazone or rosiglitazone alone, TRAP220 peptide affinity was similarly strengthened driven by a favorable change in entropy, as measured by ITC.
source: In the presence of edaglitazone or rosiglitazone alone, TRAP220 peptide affinity was similarly strengthen driven by a favorable change in entropy with binding affinities similar to OA-bound PPARγ.
evidence: This is data from ITC experiments shown in Table 4.

claim: In the fatty acid cobound scenarios, a synergetic strengthening of TRAP220 peptide affinity was observed, more than in the presence of each ligand individually, which was also driven by a favorable change in entropy, as measured by ITC.
source: In the fatty acid cobound scenarios, a synergetic strengthening of TRAP220 peptide affinity was observed, more than in the presence of each ligand individually, which was also driven by a favorable change in entropy.
evidence: This is data from ITC experiments shown in Table 4.

claim: The entropic-driven nature of the cobinding influence on TRAP220 binding is consistent with NMR and MD data indicating that C9 cobinding with an orthosteric TZD stabilizes the conformation of the AF-2 binding surface.
source: The entropic-driven nature of the cobinding influence on TRAP220 binding is consistent with our NMR and MD data, which indicate that C9 cobinding with an orthosteric TZD stabilizes the conformation of the AF-2 binding surface.
evidence: This is an interpretation that integrates ITC, NMR, and MD data.

claim: Ligand cobinding of a noncovalent synthetic ligand with natural or endogenous ligand affects PPARγ function.
source: These ITC data confirm that ligand cobinding of a noncovalent synthetic ligand with natural or endogenous ligand affects PPARγ function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ITC data.

claim: AA and OA were among the most abundant UFAs identified using mass spectrometry metabolomics as endogenous ligands present in 3T3-L1 preadipocyte cells and mouse brain and adipose tissue that bind to PPARγ.
source: AA and OA, which we used in our structural and biochemical cobinding studies, were among the most abundant UFAs identified using a mass spectrometry metabolomics approach as endogenous ligands present in 3T3-L1 preadipocyte cells and mouse brain and adipose tissue that bind to PPARγ (Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: When exogenous AA and OA were added to cells, no change in PPARγ transcription was observed.
source: However, when we added exogenous AA and OA to cells, no change in PPARγ transcription was observed (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is data from a cell-based luciferase reporter assay shown in Figure 11A.

claim: The exogenously added UFAs are already present within cells, which contributes to the basal PPARγ transcriptional activity in the absence of an exogenous ligand.
source: These observations together indicate that the exogenously added UFAs are already present within cells, which contributes to the basal PPARγ transcriptional activity in the absence of an exogenous ligand; therefore the exogenously added UFAs cause no further increases in PPARγ transcription.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cell-based assay data.

claim: Mutants (R288A, S342A, K265A, R288A/S342A, R288A/S342A/K265A) showed lower basal transcriptional activity in cells treated with DMSO control.
source: In cells treated with DMSO control, both mutants showed lower basal transcriptional activity (Figure 11B) without affecting PPARγ protein levels in cells (Figure 11—figure supplement 1) or coactivator affinity (Figure 11—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is data from a cell-based luciferase reporter assay shown in Figure 11B and supplementary figures.

claim: The mutants may reduce the binding of and activation by endogenous ligands present in cells.
source: When considered with our biochemical studies, this suggests that the mutants may reduce the binding of and activation by endogenous ligands present in cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cell-based assay data in the context of the biochemical studies.

claim: Relative to wild-type PPARγ, the mutants showed reduced activity when cells were treated with saturating synthetic TZD concentrations.
source: Relative to wild-type PPARγ, the mutants showed reduced activity when cells were treated with saturating synthetic TZD concentrations (Figure 11B).
evidence: This is data from a cell-based luciferase reporter assay shown in Figure 11B.

claim: The reduction in activity caused by the mutants is not due to decreased TZD affinity because concentration-dependent experiments showed that TZD potency was similar for wild-type PPARγ and the mutants.
source: The reduction in activity caused by the mutants is not due to decreased TZD affinity because concentration-dependent experiments showed that TZD potency was similar for wild-type PPARγ and the mutants (Figure 11C).
evidence: This is data from a cell-based luciferase reporter assay shown in Figure 11C.

claim: Cobinding of endogenous ligands and synthetic TZDs may synergistically activate PPARγ transcription over the activity of a single ligand alone.
source: When considered with all of the above studies, these data indicate that cobinding of endogenous ligands and synthetic TZDs may synergistically activate PPARγ transcription over the activity of a single ligand alone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell-based assay data in the context of all the other studies.

claim: The binding of a synthetic nuclear receptor ligand can push aside and cobind with a pre-bound endogenous ligand.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first mechanistic description showing that the binding of a synthetic nuclear receptor ligand binding can push aside and cobind with a pre-bound endogenous ligand.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: This ligand cobinding mechanism is particularly evident in crystallography studies whereby co-crystals of UFA-bound PPARγ, where the UFA crystallized in the orthosteric pocket, was pushed to an alternate site when the crystals were soaked with synthetic ligand.
source: This mechanism is particularly evident in our crystallography studies whereby co-crystals of UFA-bound PPARγ, where the UFA crystallized in the orthosteric pocket, was pushed to an alternate site when the crystals were soaked with synthetic ligand.
evidence: This is a description of the crystallography experiments.

claim: The ligand cobinding mechanism bridges or extends the reach of synthetic ligand within the orthosteric pocket with residues near and within the flexible Ω-loop region.
source: This ligand cobinding mechanism bridges or extends the reach of synthetic ligand within the orthosteric pocket with residues near and within the flexible Ω-loop region that is important in regulating PPARγ structure and function (Waku et al., 2009a; Waku et al., 2009b; Jang et al., 2017; Bae et al., 2016; Puhl et al., 2012; Waku et al., 2010), which is supported by our coregulator interaction assays and particularly our ITC studies that show cobinding of an endogenous UFA and synthetic TZD ligand synergistically improves coactivator affinity compared to each ligand alone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study, supported by citations and the ITC data.

claim: Serotonin and fatty acid metabolites were shown to synergistically bind to different arms of the orthosteric pocket of PPARγ.
source: Serotonin and fatty acid metabolites were shown to synergistically bind to different arms of the orthosteric pocket (Waku et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: MCFAs and long-chain oxidized fatty acids were shown to bind in up to three equivalents of the same ligand bound to different arms of the orthosteric pocket of PPARγ.
source: MCFAs and long-chain oxidized fatty acids were also shown bind in up to three equivalents of the same ligand bound to different arms of the orthosteric pocket (Itoh et al., 2008; Liberato et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Some synthetic ligands optimized to bind to the orthosteric pocket with high affinity can also bind a second equivalent to the alternate site at lower affinity.
source: We have shown that some synthetic ligands optimized to bind to the orthosteric pocket with high affinity can also bind a second equivalent to the alternate site at lower affinity (Hughes et al., 2016; Li et al., 2008b; Hughes et al., 2014); or one equivalent to the alternate site with an orthosteric antagonist or an oxidized lipid covalently bound to the orthosteric pocket (Hughes et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies by the authors.

claim: A crystal structure of PPARγ showed that luteolin can bind to the alternate site cobound with myristic acid that copurified during protein expression.
source: Similar to our synthetic ligand alternate binding observations, a crystal structure of PPARγ that showed that a plant-based natural product (luteolin) can bind to the alternate site cobound with a bacterial saturated 14-carbon fatty acid (myristic acid) that copurified during protein expression (Puhl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Molecular simulations showed that luteolin bound to the alternate site stabilizes the Ω-loop, and the cobinding is mediated in part through a water bridged hydrogen bond.
source: Molecular simulations showed that luteolin bound to the alternate site stabilizes the Ω-loop, and the cobinding is mediated in part through a water bridged hydrogen bond, similar to our cobinding molecular simulations with edaglitazone bound to the orthosteric pocket and C9 bound to the alternate site.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and comparison to the current study's MD simulations.

claim: RORγ can cobind a synthetic allosteric ligand and the natural ligand cholesterol in the orthosteric pocket.
source: In studies on other nuclear receptors, RORγ can cobind a synthetic allosteric ligand and the natural ligand cholesterol in the orthosteric pocket (Scheepstra et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: A study on PXR revealed orthosteric cobinding of a pharmaceutical oestrogen and an organochlorine pesticide.
source: whereas a study on PXR revealed orthosteric cobinding of a pharmaceutical oestrogen and an organochlorine pesticide (Delfosse et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: A synthetic PPARγ ligand pushes a bound endogenous UFA to an alternate site upon binding rather than completely displacing it.
source: Through a series of crystal structures we mechanistically show that a synthetic PPARγ ligand, including one used as an FDA-approved drug in the treatment of type 2 diabetes, pushes a bound endogenous UFA to an alternate site upon binding rather than completely displacing it.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the crystal structure data.

claim: The synthetic ligand displays higher affinity than the UFA for the orthosteric pocket, but the UFA also has moderate or reasonable affinity for other portions of the pocket (i.e., the alternate site).
source: This likely occurs because the synthetic ligand displays higher affinity than the UFA for the orthosteric pocket, but the UFA also has moderate or reasonable affinity, rather than weak or no affinity, for other portions of the pocket (i.e., the alternate site).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the binding data.

claim: The cobound fatty acid in the alternate site is structurally close to two other important surfaces: the RXRα DNA-binding domain interaction surface and the S245 phosphorylation surface.
source: The cobound fatty acid in the alternate site, which is located near the β-strand surface and Ω-loop region, is structurally close to two other important surfaces. In a crystal structure of the intact PPARγ/RXRα heterodimer bound to DNA (Chandra et al., 2008), there is a long-range interaction between this region in PPARγ and the RXRα DNA-binding domain (DBD). It is possible that ligand cobinding could allosterically affect or synergize with this long-range interaction. Furthermore, the alternate site where the cobound fatty acid is bound is structurally close to a surface containing S245 (S273 in PPARγ isoform 1), which is phosphorylated by the kinase Cdk5 (Choi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a structural observation supported by a citation.

claim: The antidiabetic efficacy of PPARγ-binding ligands is linked to inhibiting the phosphorylation of S245 by Cdk5.
source: The antidiabetic efficacy of PPARγ-binding ligands is linked to inhibiting this phosphorylation event (Choi et al., 2010; Choi et al., 2011), and occupancy of the alternate site can specifically inhibit this phosphorylation event (Bae et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: A cobound endogenous ligand at the alternate site may contribute to the antidiabetic efficacy of a synthetic ligand bound to the orthosteric pocket.
source: It is possible that a cobound endogenous ligand at the alternate site may contribute to the antidiabetic efficacy of a synthetic ligand bound to the orthosteric pocket.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings.

claim: It is difficult to study possible cellular functional effects of synthetic and endogenous ligand cobinding because it is not possible to control the presence of endogenous ligands as one can with synthetic ligands.
source: However, it is difficult to study possible cellular functional effects of synthetic and endogenous ligand cobinding because it is not possible to control the presence of endogenous ligands as one can with synthetic ligands.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The ligand cobinding mechanism discovered for PPARγ may be broadly applicable to other nuclear receptors and other ligand-binding proteins.
source: The ligand cobinding mechanism we discovered here for PPARγ may be broadly applicable to other nuclear receptors and other ligand-binding proteins.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings.

claim: Many nuclear receptors have been shown to interact with and/or be functionally modulated by fatty acids.
source: For example, many nuclear receptors, including ones not normally thought to be fatty acid responsive, have been shown to interact with and/or be functionally modulated by fatty acids.
evidence: This is supported by the list of nuclear receptors and citations provided in the manuscript.

claim: Fatty acids are considered to be the ancestral nuclear receptor ligands.
source: In fact, fatty acids are considered to the ancestral nuclear receptor ligands (Sumida, 1995)
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Fatty acids interact with and regulate the function of a variety of other protein targets including kinases, GPCRs, and ion channels.
source: and also interact with and regulate the function of a variety of other protein targets including kinases (McPhail et al., 1984; Murakami and Routtenberg, 1985; Khan et al., 1995), GPCRs (Stoddart et al., 2008; Yonezawa et al., 2013), and ion channels (Ordway et al., 1991; Antollini and Barrantes, 2016), which are targets (or putative targets) of synthetic ligands and clinically used drugs.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: It is estimated that most proteins likely bind endogenous metabolites.
source: More broadly, fatty acids and lipids are just one type of endogenous metabolite present in cells and it is estimated that most proteins likely bind endogenous metabolites (Lindsley and Rutter, 2006; Gallego et al., 2010; Li et al., 2010; Li and Snyder, 2011; Orsak et al., 2012; Link et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The concept of synthetic ligand/drug cobinding with endogenous metabolites to targets may be more likely than not.
source: Thus, the concept of synthetic ligand/drug cobinding with endogenous metabolites to targets may be more likely than not.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings and the prevalence of endogenous metabolite binding.
